intro: Founded in 1807, Piqua's housing stock is industrial-era — much of it decades old — and its low-lying areas near the Great Miami River and canal-era infrastructure stay damp. Chronic basement moisture is the city's most common mold driver: seepage through old foundations, sump systems that can't keep up in wet springs, and contents stored on damp basement floors. Around Fort Piqua Plaza and downtown, aging commercial-residential buildings add roof-leak attic calls.
moldNote: Piqua's mold risk is groundwater-driven: low-lying river-adjacent neighborhoods, industrial-era foundations that seep every spring, and basements used as storage on damp floors.

problemCards.title: Chronic basement moisture
problemCards.body: Low-lying areas near the river keep basements damp for months — seepage, wicking, and humid air feeding growth.

problemCards.title: Old-foundation seepage
problemCards.body: Pre-1970 foundations with failing waterproofing let spring stormwater straight in.

problemCards.title: Crawl-space dampness
problemCards.body: Damp soil and poor drainage under older homes keep crawl spaces wet year-round.
